```{r setup, include=FALSE}
library(dplyr)
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = FALSE, warning = FALSE, message = FALSE,
  fig.width = 13, fig.height = 7, dpi = 180, fig.retina = 1, out.width = "100%")
source("../../dev/diagnostic_checks/simulation-studies/distribution-checks/plot.R")
read_results <- function(filename) read.csv(file.path(params$results_directory, filename))
conditions <- read_results("conditions.csv")
summary <- read_results("summary.csv")
paired <- read_results("paired-comparison.csv")
fits <- read_results("fits.csv")
inference <- read_results("inference.csv")
default_summary <- summary |> filter(
  (check %in% c("residual", "both") & reference == "fitted-centred") |
    (check == "outcome" & reference == "fitted"),
  (view == "pooled" & role == "Pooled") | (view == "roles" & role == "All"))
# Main conditions: Gaussian and negative-binomial models, one occasion, dyad SD 0.6.
main_only <- function(data) filter(data, n_times == 1, dyad_sd == .6, family != "ordinal")
severe_scenarios <- c("omitted_partner", "heteroscedastic", "dispersion_severe")
# Checkpoints are read alphabetically (1, 10, 11, ...), so sort every table.
arrange_conditions <- function(data, ...) arrange(data, family, n_times, dyad_sd,
  match(scenario, distribution_scenario_order), n_dyads, ...)
format_rate <- function(rate, lower, upper, checked) {
  ifelse(checked == 0, "Unavailable", sprintf("%.1f%% (%.1f–%.1f), n = %s",
    100 * rate, 100 * lower, 100 * upper, checked))
}
# Any flag without and with predictor pages, side by side.
rate_table <- function(data) {
  data |> filter(statistic %in% c("any", "any_pages")) |>
    arrange_conditions(view, match(check, c("residual", "outcome", "both"))) |>
    mutate(Family = unname(distribution_family_labels[family]),
      Setting = paste0(scenario_label, ifelse(n_times > 1, ", six occasions", ""),
        ifelse(dyad_sd > .6, ", dyad SD 1.2", "")),
      View = ifelse(view == "pooled", "Pooled", "Either role"),
      Check = recode(check, residual = "Residuals", outcome = "Outcomes", both = "Both checks"),
      Rate = format_rate(rate, rate_lower, rate_upper, checked)) |>
    select(Family, Setting, n_dyads, View, Check, statistic, Rate) |>
    tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = statistic, values_from = Rate)
}
```

## Summary

```{r summary-numbers}
percent_range <- function(rate) paste0(paste(unique(sprintf("%.0f", 100 * range(rate))),
  collapse = "–"), "%")
correct_panels <- summary |> filter(scenario == "correct",
  reference %in% c("fitted-centred", "fitted"), statistic %in% names(distribution_panel_labels))
panel_maximum <- max(correct_panels$rate[correct_panels$role %in% c("Pooled", "A", "B")], na.rm = TRUE)
panel_maximum_roles <- max(correct_panels$rate[correct_panels$role == "All" &
  correct_panels$view == "roles"], na.rm = TRUE)
correct_any <- filter(default_summary, scenario == "correct", check == "both")
correct_range <- function(view_name, union = "any") with(filter(correct_any,
  view == view_name, statistic == union), percent_range(rate))
detection <- default_summary |> main_only() |>
  filter(check == "both", statistic == "any", view == "roles")
detected <- function(n, scenarios, keep = TRUE)
  detection$rate[detection$n_dyads == n & (detection$scenario %in% scenarios) == keep]
# Single panels in either role at 400 dyads; each scenario has one such condition.
flag_rate <- function(scenario_name, statistic_name) summary |>
  filter(scenario == scenario_name, statistic == statistic_name, n_dyads == 400,
    view == "roles", role == "All", reference %in% c("fitted-centred", "fitted")) |>
  pull(rate) |> distribution_percent()
coverage_range <- function(scenario_name) with(filter(main_only(inference),
  scenario == scenario_name, n_dyads == 400), percent_range(coverage))
centring <- paired |> filter(family != "ordinal", check == "residual", statistic == "any",
  (view == "pooled" & role == "Pooled") | (view == "roles" & role == "All"))
centring_change <- function(correct) with(filter(centring, (scenario == "correct") == correct),
  sprintf("%.0f", 100 * range(centred_minus_uncentred)))
```

The study uses `r unique(conditions$repetitions)` datasets per condition and
`r format(unique(conditions$reference_draws), big.mark = ",")` reference simulations per dataset.

- **Single panels rarely flag a correct model, but flags add up.** Each panel
  flagged at most `r distribution_percent(panel_maximum)` of datasets under
  correct models, pooled or within one role, and at most
  `r distribution_percent(panel_maximum_roles)` in either role (flagged in at
  least one role). In the settings
  studied, at least one flag appeared in `r correct_range("pooled")`
  of datasets with all observations pooled, `r correct_range("roles")` in either
  role, and `r correct_range("roles", "any_pages")` in either role with actor and
  partner predictor pages. So look for a consistent pattern, not any single flag.
- **Detection depends strongly on sample size.** With 40 dyads, most
  mismatches were hard to detect: apart from omitted role means of ±0.4
  (`r distribution_percent(detected(40, "mean_large"))`), mismatches were flagged
  in either role in `r percent_range(detected(40, c("correct", "mean_large"), FALSE))`
  of datasets, against `r percent_range(detected(40, "correct"))` under correct models.
  With 400 dyads, most were flagged in
  `r percent_range(detected(400, c("correct", "dispersion_small", "zeros_small"), FALSE))`.
  Mildly overdispersed counts (NB2 size 10) fitted as Poisson were flagged in only
  `r distribution_percent(detected(400, "dispersion_small"))`, and 10% extra zeros in
  `r distribution_percent(detected(400, "zeros_small"))`, against
  `r percent_range(detected(400, "correct"))` under correct models.
- **Each problem shows in a few panels**, listed in the help under
  [Reading flags](https://pascal-kueng.github.io/dyadMLM/reference/plot.dyadMLM_residual_check.html#reading-flags).
  At 400 dyads in either role, for example, 25% extra zeros flagged the QQ
  envelope in `r flag_rate("zeros_large", "qq")` of datasets but the number of zeros in
  `r flag_rate("zeros_large", "zeros")`, and an omitted partner effect (dyad SD
  1.2) flagged the PIT quartiles across the partner's predictor in
  `r flag_rate("omitted_partner", "partner_quantiles")` but the QQ
  envelope in `r flag_rate("omitted_partner", "qq")`. Panels suggest possible
  problems, not their cause.
- **A flag, or its absence, does not show whether estimates or SEs are wrong.**
  Harm depended on the kind of mismatch. At 400 dyads, omitted role means of ±0.4
  were flagged in either role in `r distribution_percent(detected(400, "mean_large"))` of datasets,
  yet actor and partner intervals covered `r coverage_range("mean_large")`
  (predictors were distributed alike in both roles). NB2 size 10 fitted as
  Poisson lowered coverage to `r coverage_range("dispersion_small")` but was
  flagged in only `r distribution_percent(detected(400, "dispersion_small"))`.
  After a flag, fit the model the pattern suggests and compare the estimates and
  SEs you report.
- **Centring adds a few false alarms and helps detect some mismatches.** Median
  centring, which moves each dataset's PIT residuals so that their median is 0.5,
  is applied automatically when the model has a freely estimated overall location
  (not for ordinal models). It raised the residual check's flag rate by
  `r paste(centring_change(TRUE), collapse = "–")` percentage points under
  correct models and by up to `r centring_change(FALSE)[2]` under mismatches,
  mainly omitted role means and extra zeros. Residuals then lose their overall
  median shift, so single panels can flag less often. With NB2 size 1 fitted as
  Poisson, the residual check flagged up to
  `r sprintf("%.0f", -100 * min(centring$centred_minus_uncentred))` percentage
  points less often (see [Effect of median centring](#effect-of-median-centring)).

## What these plots compare

`check_dyad_residuals()` compares probability integral transform (PIT) residuals with
model simulations. A PIT residual ranks an observed outcome from 0 (low) to 1 (high)
among its simulated values. `check_dyad_outcomes()` compares distributions and
summaries on the outcome scale. We study how often their numerical panels flag
correct Gaussian, negative-binomial, and ordinal models, and how often they detect
selected model mismatches. Both checks use the **same datasets, fitted models, and
complete reference simulations**.

We compare pooling all observations with checking the two partner roles
separately. We also compare the default residual check with the same calculation
without median centring. This isolates the adjustment's effect because both
versions use identical PIT randomization.

A **flag** means that an observed single value, such as the response SD, falls
strictly outside its simulated 95% limits, or a curve leaves its global envelope
(a band built so that a correct model's whole curve stays inside in a nominal 95%
of datasets). An **any flag** rate (a union of flags) counts datasets with at least
one flagged numerical panel. Unless noted, it leaves out the predictor pages.
Rates *with predictor pages* add the PIT quartiles across the actor's and the
partner's predictor. A flag in either role counts once. Neither multiple panels
nor multiple roles have a joint 5% error rate. The ECDF display and the ordinal
category ranges are excluded from these rates.

These are descriptive checks. Fitting can make a panel flag a correct model less
often (conservative) or more often (liberal) than 5%, and more flags under a
mismatch do not alone establish a better check. Compare detection with the
correct-model results. This focused study does not validate other families,
missing-data patterns, or every form of dependence. The
[partner-dependence study](partner-dependence-simulation.html) evaluates
omitted partner correlation, and the [covariance-pooling study](covariance-pooling.html)
evaluates differences between dyad compositions.

<details>
<summary>Study design and interpretation</summary>

The main conditions use 40, 100, or 400 complete dyads, each containing roles A
and B. Standard-normal predictors correlate 0.3 between partners. Actor and
partner effects are 0.5 and 0.3. A shared normal dyad intercept has SD 0.6.
Gaussian outcomes have intercept 1 and residual SD 1. Negative-binomial (NB2) outcomes
use a log link, intercept log(3), and conditional variance
$\mu + \mu^2/k$, where $k$ is the size parameter.

Gaussian mismatches either omit role shifts of ±0.2 or ±0.4, or impose a common
residual SD when the true role SD ratio is 1.25 or 1.50. The variance conditions
keep the average residual variance at 1. Count mismatches either fit a Poisson
model to negative-binomial outcomes with size 10 or 3, or omit an extra-zero
probability of 0.10 or 0.25 from a negative-binomial model. One feature changes at
a time. The count mean before adding extra zeros is adjusted to preserve the
overall conditional expectation. The settings table below records the baseline
size and fitted family.

Correct Gaussian and negative-binomial models are also run with dyad SD 1.2 at
100 and 400 dyads. With the same dyad SD and sample sizes, three severe
mismatches distort inference (see
[below](#are-mismatches-that-distort-estimates-or-ses-detected)). Correct
five-category ordinal models use 100 and 400 dyads. Their latent outcome is the
Gaussian model's predictors and dyad intercept without the intercept 1, scaled by
$\pi/\sqrt{3}$, plus standard logistic noise, cut into categories of about
10/20/40/20/10%. Two Gaussian longitudinal conditions use 100 dyads and six
occasions, with either a correct mean model or omitted role shifts of ±0.2. They
add an independent stationary AR(1) process for each person, with SD 0.6 and
lag-one correlation 0.5, and independent residual noise with SD 0.8. The fitted
model includes the shared dyad intercept and the person-specific AR(1) process.

Reference simulations redraw all random effects while keeping predictors and
model parameters fixed. Models are not refitted within the reference simulations.
For correct Gaussian and negative-binomial models, a separate reference bank uses
the true generating parameters, without PIT centring. These known-parameter checks
are run even when fitting fails. They distinguish the behavior of the reference
calculation from the effects of estimating parameters.

Every dataset is checked with all observations pooled and with the two roles
separately, each with a page for the actor's and the partner's predictor.
Residual panels include the QQ envelope, mean PIT distance, and the PIT quartiles
across predicted outcomes and across each predictor. Outcome panels include the
response SD (after subtracting fixed-effect predictions), largest absolute
deviation, number of zeros where available, and, for ordinal outcomes, the
category ranges.

Rates use available checks. Failed fits, convergence or Hessian problems, and
failed checks are recorded and excluded without retry. Known-parameter and
fitted-reference rates can therefore have different denominators. Bars show 95%
Wilson intervals for Monte Carlo uncertainty.
Counts and uncertainty are reported following the guidance of
[Morris et al. (2019)](https://doi.org/10.1002/sim.8086).

The report reads saved CSV files and does not fit models. See the
[study code](https://github.com/Pascal-Kueng/dyadMLM/blob/main/dev/diagnostic_checks/simulation-studies/distribution-checks/run.R),
[plot code](https://github.com/Pascal-Kueng/dyadMLM/blob/main/dev/diagnostic_checks/simulation-studies/distribution-checks/plot.R),
and [study notes](https://github.com/Pascal-Kueng/dyadMLM/blob/main/dev/diagnostic_checks/simulation-studies/README.md).

```{r settings}
conditions |> arrange_conditions() |>
  group_by(family, scenario, scenario_label, role_mean, sd_ratio, nb_size,
    zero_probability, fit_family, dyad_sd, n_times) |>
  summarise(dyads = paste(n_dyads, collapse = " / "), .groups = "drop") |>
  arrange(family, n_times, dyad_sd, match(scenario, distribution_scenario_order)) |>
  transmute(family = unname(distribution_family_labels[family]), scenario_label,
    role_mean, sd_ratio, nb_size = ifelse(family == "Negative binomial", nb_size, NA_real_),
    zero_probability, fit_family, dyad_sd, n_times, dyads) |>
  knitr::kable(col.names = c("Generated family", "Setting", "Role shift (±)",
    "SD ratio", "NB2 size", "Extra-zero probability", "Fitted family", "Dyad SD",
    "Occasions", "Dyads"), digits = 2)
```

</details>

## Correct models

Each row below is one numerical panel with all observations pooled. Grey points
use known parameters, blue points use the fitted model with the package defaults,
and orange points omit PIT centring. The dashed line marks 5% as a benchmark,
not a guaranteed fitted-model flag rate. The outcome summaries do not depend on
PIT centring, and ordinal PIT residuals are never centred.

```{r correct-panels, fig.height=9, fig.alt='Individual-panel flag rates under correct Gaussian, negative-binomial, and ordinal models, comparing known parameters, fitted defaults, and uncentred fitted PIT residuals.'}
plot_distribution_panels(summary)
known <- summary |> filter(reference == "known", role != "All",
  statistic %in% names(distribution_panel_labels), checked > 0)
percent <- function(rate) sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * rate)
fitted_levels <- default_summary |> filter(scenario == "correct", view == "pooled",
    statistic %in% c("response_sd", "zeros", "mean_distance")) |>
  group_by(statistic) |> summarise(rate = max(rate, na.rm = TRUE))
fitted_level <- function(name) percent(fitted_levels$rate[fitted_levels$statistic == name])
```

With known parameters, the limits come from the model that generated the data,
so each panel should flag at most about 5% of datasets. Across all
`r nrow(known)` known-parameter rates, the average is `r percent(mean(known$rate))`.
This checks the implementation. It is not a finding about fitted references.

With fitted models and all observations pooled, the response SD, number of zeros,
and mean PIT distance flag in at most `r fitted_level("response_sd")`,
`r fitted_level("zeros")`, and `r fitted_level("mean_distance")` of datasets.
The fitted model already matches these overall levels.

Reading every numerical panel of both checks for both roles, without the predictor
pages, at least one flag appears in `r correct_range("roles")` of datasets under every
correct model. With all observations pooled, this is `r correct_range("pooled")`.

<details>
<summary>Any flags under correct models</summary>

The table counts any numerical flag within each check, or across both checks.
The latter is a union within each dataset, not a sum of the two rates. Role-based
rates count either role, and their additional comparisons can increase the rate.
Each entry gives the percentage, its 95% Wilson interval, and the denominator.

```{r correct-any}
default_summary |> main_only() |> filter(scenario == "correct") |> rate_table() |>
  knitr::kable(col.names = c("Family", "Setting", "Dyads", "View", "Check",
    "Any flag", "With predictor pages"))
```

</details>

## Detecting model mismatches

The plots count any numerical flag for each default check. Solid lines count a
flag in either role, while dotted lines pool all observations. These are different
sets of comparisons, so the role-based check may flag more often even under a
correct model. Grey lines repeat the correct-model rate of the same check and
view, the false-alarm baseline.

```{r gaussian-detection, fig.alt='Gaussian mismatch detection by sample size, comparing pooled and role-based residual and outcome checks with the correct-model baseline.'}
plot_distribution_detection(summary, "gaussian")
pooled_outcome <- default_summary |> main_only() |> filter(family == "gaussian",
    check == "outcome", view == "pooled", statistic == "any") |>
  group_by(correct = scenario == "correct") |>
  summarise(rate = max(rate, na.rm = TRUE))
```

Pooled outcome checks flag at most
`r distribution_percent(pooled_outcome$rate[!pooled_outcome$correct])` of datasets
under these Gaussian mismatches and at most
`r distribution_percent(pooled_outcome$rate[pooled_outcome$correct])` under the
correct model. The fitted model already reproduces the pooled SD, so pooled
outcome summaries have little to detect.

```{r count-detection, fig.alt='Negative-binomial mismatch detection by sample size, comparing pooled and role-based residual and outcome checks with the correct-model baseline.'}
plot_distribution_detection(summary, "nbinom2")
```

The tables show how often each panel flags each mismatch in either role, as
percentages of datasets at 40 / 100 / 400 dyads with the package defaults. The
correct-model column is the false-alarm baseline.

```{r panel-detection, results='asis'}
separator <- " / " # Narrow no-break spaces keep each entry on one line.
panel_rates <- function(rate, checked) if (all(checked == 0)) NA else
  paste(ifelse(checked > 0, round(100 * rate), "–"), collapse = separator)
for (family_name in c("gaussian", "nbinom2")) {
  rates <- default_summary |> main_only() |> filter(family == family_name,
      view == "roles", statistic %in% names(distribution_panel_labels)) |>
    arrange_conditions()
  settings <- unique(rates$scenario_label)
  rates |> group_by(scenario_label, statistic) |>
    summarise(Rates = panel_rates(rate, checked), .groups = "drop") |>
    filter(!is.na(Rates)) |>
    tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = scenario_label, values_from = Rates) |>
    arrange(match(statistic, names(distribution_panel_labels))) |>
    mutate(statistic = distribution_panel_labels[statistic]) |>
    select(statistic, all_of(settings)) |>
    knitr::kable(col.names = c("Panel", settings),
      caption = paste(distribution_family_labels[family_name], "models")) |> print()
}
rates_at <- function(family_name, scenario_name, check_name, statistic_name, view_name = "roles")
  default_summary |> main_only() |> filter(family == family_name, scenario == scenario_name,
      check == check_name, statistic == statistic_name, view == view_name,
      n_dyads %in% c(100, 400)) |>
    arrange(n_dyads) |> pull(rate) |> distribution_percent() |> paste(collapse = separator)
```

The main patterns, at 100 / 400 dyads in either role unless noted:

- **Omitted role means** show mainly in the role view of residual checks (±0.2:
  `r rates_at("gaussian", "mean_small", "residual", "any")`). The pooled residual
  view and the outcome checks' numerical panels (not the ECDF) stay near their
  correct-model rates
  (`r rates_at("gaussian", "mean_small", "residual", "any", "pooled")` versus
  `r rates_at("gaussian", "correct", "residual", "any", "pooled")`, and
  `r rates_at("gaussian", "mean_small", "outcome", "any")` versus
  `r rates_at("gaussian", "correct", "outcome", "any")`). The exception is the
  per-role response SD at ±0.4 (`r rates_at("gaussian", "mean_large", "outcome", "response_sd")`),
  which reacts to the inflated fitted residual SD.
- **Role SD differences** show most in the per-role response SD and mean PIT
  distance (ratio 1.50: `r rates_at("gaussian", "variance_large", "outcome", "response_sd")`
  and `r rates_at("gaussian", "variance_large", "residual", "mean_distance")`).
- **NB2 overdispersion fitted as Poisson** is partly absorbed by a larger fitted
  dyad SD (see below). Residual checks flag either role in
  `r rates_at("nbinom2", "dispersion_large", "residual", "any")` of datasets for
  size 3, compared with `r rates_at("nbinom2", "correct", "residual", "any")`
  under the correct model.
- **Omitted zero inflation** shows most in the PIT QQ envelope and the PIT
  quartiles across predicted outcomes (25% extra zeros:
  `r rates_at("nbinom2", "zeros_large", "residual", "qq")` and
  `r rates_at("nbinom2", "zeros_large", "residual", "predicted_quantiles")`). The number of zeros stays
  weak (`r rates_at("nbinom2", "zeros_large", "outcome", "zeros")`) because a
  smaller fitted NB2 size absorbs the extra zeros (see below).

<details>
<summary>What the fitted models estimate</summary>

A fitted model can absorb part of a mismatch into its estimates (medians over
usable fits). The data have dyad SD 0.6 and, for Gaussian outcomes, average
residual variance 1.

```{r fitted-estimates}
fit_at_400 <- function(family_name, scenario_name, column) {
  row <- fits |> main_only() |> filter(reference == "fitted", family == family_name,
    scenario == scenario_name, n_dyads == 400)
  sprintf("%.2f", row[[column]])
}
```

At 400 dyads, omitted role means of ±0.4 give a residual SD of
`r fit_at_400("gaussian", "mean_large", "median_dispersion")`, compared with
`r fit_at_400("gaussian", "correct", "median_dispersion")` under the correct model.
Poisson fits to NB2 data with size 3 give a dyad SD of
`r fit_at_400("nbinom2", "dispersion_large", "median_dyad_sd")`, compared with
`r fit_at_400("nbinom2", "correct", "median_dyad_sd")` under the correct count model.
With 25% omitted zero inflation, the NB2 size is
`r fit_at_400("nbinom2", "zeros_large", "median_dispersion")`, compared with
`r fit_at_400("nbinom2", "correct", "median_dispersion")` (a smaller size means
more overdispersion).

</details>

## Are mismatches that distort estimates or SEs detected?

Each fitted model gives 95% Wald intervals for the actor (0.5) and partner (0.3)
effects. **Coverage** is the percentage of intervals that contain the true value
and should be near 95%. The **SE ratio** divides the average SE by the SD of the
estimates. Below 1, the SEs are too small. Low coverage with an SE ratio near 1
means the estimates are biased. **Flagged** is the percentage of datasets with any
flag in either check and either role, without and with actor and partner
predictor pages.

Three severe mismatches were added to distort inference. Omitting the partner
effect biases the actor effect. A residual SD that rises with the actor predictor,
exp(actor − 1), makes the actor SE too small, and Poisson fits to NB2 outcomes
with size 1 make both SEs too small. These settings use 100 / 400 dyads and dyad
SD 1.2. The correct Gaussian and negative-binomial models with the same dyad SD
give their false-alarm rates.

```{r consequences-severe}
flag_rates <- default_summary |> filter(check == "both", view == "roles") |>
  select(condition, statistic, rate) |>
  tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = statistic, values_from = rate)
consequence_table <- function(selected) {
  collapse_sizes <- function(values) paste(ifelse(is.na(values), "–", values), collapse = separator)
  inference |> filter(condition %in% selected) |>
    transmute(condition, family, scenario, scenario_label, n_dyads, n_times, dyad_sd,
      term = sub("_predictor", "", term), coverage = round(100 * coverage),
      se_ratio = sprintf("%.2f", se_ratio)) |>
    tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = term, values_from = c(coverage, se_ratio)) |>
    left_join(transmute(flag_rates, condition, flagged = round(100 * any),
      flagged_pages = round(100 * any_pages)), by = "condition") |>
    arrange_conditions() |>
    group_by(family, scenario, scenario_label) |>
    summarise(across(c(coverage_actor, coverage_partner, se_ratio_actor, se_ratio_partner,
      flagged, flagged_pages), collapse_sizes), .groups = "drop") |>
    arrange(family, match(scenario, distribution_scenario_order)) |>
    mutate(family = unname(distribution_family_labels[family])) |>
    select(-scenario) |>
    knitr::kable(col.names = c("Family", "Setting", "Actor coverage (%)",
      "Partner coverage (%)", "Actor SE ratio", "Partner SE ratio", "Flagged (%)",
      "With pages (%)"))
}
consequence_table(conditions$condition[conditions$n_times == 1 & conditions$dyad_sd > .6])
```

The main mismatches, at 40 / 100 / 400 dyads:

```{r consequences-main}
consequence_table(main_only(conditions)$condition)
```

## Effect of median centring

```{r centring-loss}
loss <- paired |> filter(scenario != "correct", n_dyads == 400,
    check == "residual", statistic %in% names(distribution_panel_labels),
    (view == "pooled" & role == "Pooled") | (view == "roles" & role == "All")) |>
  slice_min(centred_minus_uncentred, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE)
loss_any <- summary |> filter(condition == loss$condition, view == loss$view,
    role == loss$role, check == "residual", statistic == "any") |>
  pull(rate, reference)
```

At 400 dyads, the largest drop in a single panel's flag rate after centring is
`r sprintf("%.1f", -100 * loss$centred_minus_uncentred)` percentage points, for the
"`r distribution_panel_labels[[loss$statistic]]`" panel under
"`r loss$scenario_label`" (`r ifelse(loss$view == "pooled", "pooled", "either role")`).
There, the residual check's any flag rate is
`r distribution_percent(loss_any[["fitted-uncentred"]])` without centring and
`r distribution_percent(loss_any[["fitted-centred"]])` with it.

## Additional designs and exclusions

The extra conditions check stronger dyad dependence, ordinal outcomes, and one
longitudinal model. They extend the main conditions without covering all dependence
structures.

```{r additional-designs}
default_summary |> filter(!condition %in% main_only(conditions)$condition,
    !scenario %in% severe_scenarios) |>
  rate_table() |>
  knitr::kable(col.names = c("Family", "Setting", "Dyads", "View", "Check",
    "Any flag", "With predictor pages"))
role_means <- default_summary |> filter(family == "gaussian", n_dyads == 100, dyad_sd == .6,
    check == "residual", view == "roles", statistic == "any")
role_means_rate <- function(scenario_name, occasions) distribution_percent(
  role_means$rate[role_means$scenario == scenario_name & role_means$n_times == occasions])
categories <- summary |> filter(family == "ordinal", statistic == "category_any",
    reference == "fitted", (view == "pooled" & role == "Pooled") | (view == "roles" & role == "All")) |>
  arrange(n_dyads)
category_rates <- function(view_name) paste(distribution_percent(
  categories$rate[categories$view == view_name]), collapse = separator)
```

At 100 dyads, the role view of residual checks flags omitted role means of ±0.2
in `r role_means_rate("mean_small", 6)` of datasets with six occasions (correct model:
`r role_means_rate("correct", 6)`), compared with `r role_means_rate("mean_small", 1)`
with one occasion. Six occasions give each role six times as many rows.

For correct ordinal models, at least one category fell outside its range in
`r category_rates("pooled")` of datasets pooled and `r category_rates("roles")` in
either role (100 / 400 dyads).

```{r fit-failures, results='asis'}
failed <- fits |> filter(reference == "fitted",
    (fit_errors + fit_problems) / attempted > .02) |> arrange_conditions()
if (nrow(failed)) cat("More than 2% of fits had errors or problems in: ",
  paste0(distribution_family_labels[failed$family], ", ", failed$scenario_label, ", ",
    failed$n_dyads, " dyads", ifelse(failed$n_times > 1, ", six occasions", ""),
    ifelse(failed$dyad_sd > .6, ", dyad SD 1.2", ""), " (",
    failed$fit_errors + failed$fit_problems, " of ", failed$attempted, ")", collapse = "; "),
  ". Their rates use the remaining datasets.\n", sep = "")
longitudinal <- filter(fits, n_times > 1, scenario == "correct")
problems <- longitudinal$fit_problems[longitudinal$reference == "fitted"]
```

`r if (problems > 0) paste0("In the longitudinal correct model, the ", problems, " fits with problems estimated a residual SD of at most ", sprintf("%.3f", longitudinal$maximum_problem_dispersion[longitudinal$reference == "fitted"]), ". Six occasions separate the person-level AR(1) process from independent noise only weakly. The known-parameter rates there still use all ", longitudinal$usable[longitudinal$reference == "known"], " datasets.")`

## Why not use DHARMa directly?

[DHARMa](https://CRAN.R-project.org/package=DHARMa) supports mixed models, but
its residual tests, such as the uniformity and outlier tests, assume
independent residuals. When random effects are redrawn, partners' residuals stay
correlated, so these tests' error rates need not hold, as DHARMa's help also
notes. With DHARMa's default since version 0.5.0, random effects keep their
fitted values. If they absorb all residual variation, as in APIMs fitted with
`dispformula = ~ 0`, the simulations reproduce the data almost exactly. With
random effects redrawn, grouping by dyad (`recalculateResiduals(group = dyad)`)
sums each dyad's observed and simulated values, which is valid but lets role
differences cancel. Selecting one role (`sel`) is valid for cross-sectional
dyads but not for repeated measures. The `rotation` option needs the full
residual covariance, which for non-Gaussian models usually must be estimated,
imprecisely, from the simulations. dyadMLM instead builds each panel's reference
from whole simulated datasets, which keep the fitted partner and time
dependence. This study did not compare the two approaches.

## Limitations

- Predictors were distributed alike in both roles. When predictor means differ
  by role, omitted role means can bias actor and partner effects, so their good
  coverage here need not hold.
- Actor and partner effects were the same in both roles, so the study does not
  show how well the panels reveal role-specific effects.
- The panels were chosen with earlier runs of these scenarios. This run uses new
  seeds, but the panels may detect other mismatches less well than these.
- No heavy-tailed residuals, gross outliers, or data errors were simulated, so
  the study does not show whether panels such as the QQ plot and the largest
  absolute deviation reveal them.
